title: Incorporating variation in death times improves predictions of ectotherm responses to stressful temperatures
experiments_summary:
1. **Analysis of published Drosophila knockdown data**: Published datasets for knockdown times (tf) of adults from 11 Drosophila species exposed to a series of constant stressful temperatures were used. Trials with fewer than 10 individuals were excluded. Log-logistic scale and shape parameters were estimated at each temperature per species using the R package flexsurv. Mixed-effects likelihood ratio tests assessed whether shape declined with increasing temperature. Residual analysis evaluated linearity of the TDT relationship.

2. **Model comparison at constant temperatures**: Four parametric survival models (log-logistic, Weibull, log-normal, Gompertz, and exponential) were compared using AIC to determine best fit to the Drosophila knockdown data. A proportional hazards (PH) model was also tested using a likelihood ratio test to assess whether hazard ratios were constant over time across temperatures.

3. **Comparison of failure density and survival curve predictions**: For two representative species (D. subobscura and D. equinoxialis), predicted failure time densities and cumulative survival curves from the Rezende et al. model (non-parametric average survival curve) and the increasing variance log-logistic model were compared against observed empirical distributions at low and high stressful temperatures.

4. **Validation using fluctuating temperature experiment with D. melanogaster**: Published data from an experiment subjecting 26 sets of adult D. melanogaster to fluctuating temperatures between 34 and 42 °C were used. Median failure times predicted by three models—Jørgensen et al. deterministic model, Rezende et al. probabilistic model, and the increasing variance log-logistic model—were compared to observed median failure times using sum of absolute errors for both males and females. Additionally, log-likelihood differences between the increasing variance log-logistic and Rezende et al. models were computed for each set, and a paired t-test was used to assess which model better fit the observed failure distributions across the 26 sets. A supplementary comparison of log-logistic models with constant versus increasing variance was also conducted for this population.
